title: Residue and value alternatives for one-dimensional analytic fields
statement: Let $k\subseteq E$ be complete fields with compatible nontrivial nonarchimedean real absolute values, with $k$ algebraically closed [def-weil-field]. For any such field $F$ put $F^\circ=\{a:|a|\le1\}$ [def-trf-valuation-ring], $\widetilde F=F^\circ/\{a:|a|<1\}$ and $\Gamma_F=|F^\times|\subset\mathbf R_{>0}$. For $z\in E$ write $k(z)^\wedge$ for the closure of the subfield generated by $k$ and $z$. Assume $E\ne k$ and $E$ is finite over $k(y)^\wedge$ for some $y\in E$. Then $\widetilde k$ is algebraically closed and $\Gamma_k$ is divisible (every positive integral power map is surjective). Exactly one of the following holds: (2) $\widetilde E/\widetilde k$ is finitely generated of transcendence degree one and $\Gamma_E=\Gamma_k$; (3) $\widetilde E=\widetilde k$ and $\Gamma_E=\Gamma_k r^{\mathbf Z}$ for some $r\notin\Gamma_k$; (4) $\widetilde E=\widetilde k$ and $\Gamma_E=\Gamma_k$. In case (2) there is $u\in\widetilde E$ transcendental over $\widetilde k$ such that $\widetilde E/\widetilde k(u)$ is finite separable [def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension]. Transcendence means absence of a nonzero polynomial relation; transcendence degree one means a maximal algebraically independent set has one element.

source.place: §6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42, Remark 6.2.2; first paragraph of proof of Theorem 6.3.1, p. 49 (residue separating coordinate and cyclic value coordinate).

proof.text: First $\Gamma_k$ is divisible: for $a\in k^\times$ and $m\ge1$, a root $b$ of $T^m-a$ in $k$ satisfies $|b|^m=|a|$. To see that $\widetilde k$ is algebraically closed, lift any monic nonconstant polynomial over $\widetilde k$ coefficientwise to a monic polynomial $P\in k^\circ[T]$. It has a root $b\in k$. If $|b|>1$, its leading term has absolute value strictly greater than every other term, contradicting $P(b)=0$; hence $b\in k^\circ$ and its residue is a root of the original polynomial. We use throughout the elementary consequence of the ultrametric inequality that $|a-b|<|a|$ implies $|b|=|a|$ (apply the inequality in both directions).

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: The chosen $y$ is transcendental over $k$: if algebraic, its minimal polynomial over the algebraically closed field $k$ is linear, so $y\in k$, and finiteness of $E/k$ would force $E=k$. Put $L=k(y)^\wedge$. Density makes $k(y)\subset L$ immediate, meaning equality of residue fields and value groups: for $h\in L^\times$ choose $f\in k(y)$ with $|h-f|<\min(|h|,1)$. Then $|f|=|h|$, and if $|h|\le1$ the residues of $f$ and $h$ coincide. Thus it suffices first to compute these invariants on $k(y)$.

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: Assume that the set $\{|y-a|:a\in k\}$ has a minimum $r=|y-a_0|>0$ and $r\in\Gamma_k$. Choose $b\in k^\times$ with $|b|=r$ and put $t=(y-a_0)/b$. Its residue $\bar t$ is transcendental over $\widetilde k$: otherwise algebraic closedness of $\widetilde k$ makes it equal to the residue of some $c\in k^\circ$, giving $|y-(a_0+bc)|=r|t-c|<r$, a contradiction.

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: For a nonzero polynomial $P(t)=\sum c_i t^i$, choose a coefficient $c_j$ of maximal absolute value. The polynomial $P/c_j$ has integral coefficients and a nonzero reduction, whose value at the transcendental $\bar t$ is nonzero. Consequently $|P(t)|=\max_i|c_i|$. For $P/Q$, divide both polynomials by maximal coefficients $c,d$. Then $|P/Q|=|c/d|\in\Gamma_k$; if this value is $1$, its residue is $\overline{c/d}\,\overline{P/c}(\bar t)/\overline{Q/d}(\bar t)$, and if it is $<1$ its residue is zero. Every rational function in $\bar t$ lifts by this same formula. Thus $\Gamma_L=\Gamma_k$ and $\widetilde L=\widetilde k(\bar t)$.

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: If the minimum $r=|y-a_0|$ exists but $r\notin\Gamma_k$, put $t=y-a_0$. No nonzero integral power of $r$ belongs to $\Gamma_k$: divisibility of $\Gamma_k$ and uniqueness of positive real roots would imply $r\in\Gamma_k$. The nonzero terms of every polynomial $\sum c_it^i$ therefore have distinct absolute values, and its norm equals its unique largest term. For a rational function $P/Q$ its value is $|c/d|r^{i-j}$, where $ct^i,dt^j$ are the largest terms. This equals $1$ only if $i=j$ and $|c/d|=1$; then $(P/Q)/(c/d)$ differs from $1$ by an element of norm $<1$. It follows that $\widetilde L=\widetilde k$ and $\Gamma_L=\Gamma_k r^{\mathbf Z}$.

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: If no minimum exists, write a nonzero rational function as $f(y)=c\prod_{i=1}^m(y-a_i)^{n_i}$ with $c\in k^\times$, $a_i\in k$, $n_i\in\mathbf Z$, using factorization of polynomials over $k$. Choose $a\in k$ with $|y-a|<\min_i|y-a_i|$. For each $i$, $(y-a_i)/(a-a_i)=1+(y-a)/(a-a_i)$ differs from $1$ by norm $<1$; finite products and integral powers retain this property. Hence $|f(y)/f(a)-1|<1$. Constants need no approximation. Thus $|f(y)|=|f(a)|\in\Gamma_k$, and if $|f(y)|\le1$ its residue equals that of $f(a)$. We obtain $\widetilde L=\widetilde k$ and $\Gamma_L=\Gamma_k$.

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-valued-extension-degree-bound] to the finite valued extension $E/L$: both $[\widetilde E:\widetilde L]$ and $[\Gamma_E:\Gamma_L]$ are finite. If $\Gamma_L=\Gamma_k$, every $\gamma\in\Gamma_E$ has a positive power $\gamma^m\in\Gamma_k$; extracting an $m$th root in $\Gamma_k$ and using uniqueness of positive real roots gives $\gamma\in\Gamma_k$. If also $\widetilde L=\widetilde k$, algebraic closedness forces $\widetilde E=\widetilde k$, giving case (4). If instead $\widetilde L=\widetilde k(\bar t)$, a finite basis of $\widetilde E$ over this rational field is a finite set of field generators over it. Thus $\widetilde E/\widetilde k$ is finitely generated of transcendence degree one, giving case (2).

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: In the remaining case $\Gamma_L=\Gamma_k r^{\mathbf Z}$ and $\widetilde L=\widetilde k$, [lem-trf-valued-extension-degree-bound] again gives $\widetilde E=\widetilde k$ and finite index $e=[\Gamma_E:\Gamma_L]$. Put $N=e!$. For every $\gamma\in\Gamma_E$, its class modulo $\Gamma_L$ is killed by $N$, so $\gamma^N=c r^m$ with $c\in\Gamma_k$ and $m\in\mathbf Z$. Taking roots in $\Gamma_k$ gives $\Gamma_E\subseteq\Gamma_k r^{(1/N)\mathbf Z}$. Set $J=\{j\in\mathbf Z:r^{j/N}\in\Gamma_E\}$. It contains $N\mathbf Z$. If $d$ is its least positive element, Euclidean division shows $J=d\mathbf Z$. Hence $\Gamma_E=\Gamma_k s^{\mathbf Z}$ for $s=r^{d/N}\in\Gamma_E$. If $s\in\Gamma_k$, then $r^d=s^N\in\Gamma_k$ would force $r\in\Gamma_k$, impossible. This is case (3).

source.place: Section 6.2 opening, printed pp. 41–42; Remark 6.2.2; proof of Theorem 6.3.1, first paragraph, printed p. 49. Agent-supplied elementary rational-function computations; local PDF unavailable.

proof.text: In case (2), apply [lem-weil-pbc-algclosed-fg-field-separating-basis] with ground field $\widetilde k$ and extension $\widetilde E$. Step 1 supplies algebraic closedness and step 7 supplies finite generation. Since the transcendence degree is one, the separating basis consists of a single element $u$. The cited statement makes $\widetilde E/\widetilde k(u)$ separable algebraic. It is finite: take finitely many field generators for $\widetilde E/\widetilde k$, which also generate over $\widetilde k(u)$, and bound the powers of each using its monic minimal polynomial; the resulting finite list of monomials spans. This proves the last assertion.

proof.text: The three cases are pairwise disjoint: case (2) has positive residue transcendence degree whereas (3) and (4) have equal residue fields; (3) has a value strictly outside $\Gamma_k$ whereas (4) has equal value groups. Steps 3–8 prove that at least one case occurs. Thus exactly one occurs.
